subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the Edexcel spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Edexcel Sociology simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: The key difference between crime and deviance is that...
options: Crime breaks the law; deviance breaks social norms (which may not be illegal)
questions.explain: Crime breaks the law and is punishable; deviance breaks norms and may or may not be illegal.

questions.q: Talking loudly to yourself in a quiet library is best described as...
questions.explain: It breaks social norms without breaking the law, so it is deviant but not criminal.

questions.q: The idea that whether an act is deviant depends on the time, place and society shows that deviance is...
questions.explain: Deviance is relative/socially constructed: it varies between societies and over time.

questions.q: 'Informal social control' is exercised by...
options: Agents like family, peers and friends through approval or disapproval
questions.explain: Informal social control uses everyday sanctions from family, friends and peers, not official agencies.

questions.q: A teenager avoiding shoplifting because their parents would be ashamed is an example of...
questions.explain: Fear of family disapproval is informal social control.

questions.q: Durkheim argued that a limited amount of crime is...
options: Functional/inevitable and can benefit society (e.g. reinforcing norms)
questions.explain: Durkheim saw crime as inevitable and even functional: it clarifies norms and can promote social change.

questions.q: Durkheim's term for a state of normlessness, where social norms break down, is...
questions.explain: Anomie is Durkheim's concept of normlessness, when shared rules weaken.

questions.q: Merton's strain theory explains crime as resulting from...
options: A gap between society's goals (e.g. wealth) and the legitimate means to achieve them
questions.explain: Merton argued strain arises when people cannot achieve shared goals (like wealth) by legitimate means.

questions.q: In Merton's theory, a person who turns to crime to gain wealth they cannot earn legally is an...
questions.explain: An 'innovator' accepts society's goals but uses illegitimate means to reach them.

questions.q: Howard Becker argued that deviance is...
options: Created by the reaction of others who apply a label
A quality of the act itself
questions.explain: Becker (labelling theory) argued no act is inherently deviant until others label it so.

questions.q: Becker's idea that a deviant label (e.g. 'criminal') overrides all other identities is called a...
questions.explain: A master status is a label so powerful it dominates how others see the person.

questions.q: Which of the following is a main source used to measure crime in England and Wales?
questions.explain: Police recorded crime is one of the two main official measures of crime.

questions.q: The Crime Survey for England and Wales (a victim survey) is useful because it...
options: Only counts crimes reported to police
Can reveal crimes not reported to or recorded by the police
questions.explain: Victim surveys capture unreported crime, helping reveal the true extent of crime.

questions.q: The 'dark figure of crime' refers to...
options: Crime that is unreported and/or unrecorded, so missing from official statistics
questions.explain: The dark figure is the hidden crime not captured in official statistics.

questions.q: A reason official crime statistics may be unreliable is that...
options: Some victims do not report crimes and police may not record them all
questions.explain: Under-reporting and inconsistent recording make official statistics an incomplete picture.

questions.q: Official statistics generally show that recorded offenders are more likely to be...
questions.explain: Statistically, young males are over-represented among recorded offenders.

questions.q: 'White-collar crime' committed by professionals (e.g. fraud) is often under-represented in statistics because it is...
options: Hard to detect and less likely to be reported
questions.explain: White-collar crime is often hidden and hard to detect, so it is under-recorded.

questions.q: Marxists argue that the law and criminal justice system tend to...
options: Serve the interests of the ruling class and focus on working-class crime
questions.explain: Marxists argue laws protect ruling-class interests and enforcement targets working-class crime more.

questions.q: A 'moral panic' (Cohen) occurs when the media...
options: Exaggerate a group's behaviour, creating public fear and 'folk devils'
questions.explain: A moral panic is media-driven exaggeration that turns a group into 'folk devils' and heightens public anxiety.

questions.q: Prisons, the police and the courts are examples of agencies of...
questions.explain: These official agencies with legal powers exercise formal social control.
